changeLog.note: Initial original authoring to schema v1.0
Editorial rewrite of advisor and client prose; substance unchanged.

advisor.summary: Concentrating several years of planned giving into a single donor-advised-fund contribution converts gifts that were vanishing under the standard deduction into a deduction that actually itemizes, while grants to the client's charities keep their normal schedule. Two OBBBA changes sharpen the 2026 math: the 60-percent-of-AGI ceiling for cash gifts to public charities is now permanent, and the new 0.5-percent-of-AGI floor of §170(b)(1)(I) disallows the first slice of charitable deductions in every itemizing year — a haircut a bunching cycle pays once rather than annually. Funding with long-term appreciated securities adds the second engine: a fair-market-value deduction with the built-in gain never recognized, subject to the 30 percent ceiling. The model adds the contribution to itemized charitable deductions; AGI-limit headroom and the floor are reviewed outside it.
mechanics: Against the 2026 MFJ standard deduction of $32,200, steady annual gifts often earn little marginal benefit; concentrating three years of giving into one DAF contribution itemizes decisively in the bunch year, with the standard deduction claimed in the off years — more total deduction across the cycle for identical generosity.

A contribution to a donor-advised fund described in §4966(d)(2) completes the gift at once: the deduction lands at contribution even though grants to operating charities are advised out over the years that follow.

Long-term appreciated publicly traded securities deduct at fair market value with the gain never recognized; the 30 percent ceiling for capital-gain property and the permanent 60 percent ceiling for cash each carry a five-year carryforward for the excess under §170(d)(1).

For tax years beginning after 2025, §170(b)(1)(I) disallows itemized charitable deductions up to 0.5 percent of the contribution base — at $400,000 of AGI, the first $2,000 of gifts each itemizing year — which is precisely why fewer, larger itemizing years now win; amounts lost solely to the floor carry forward.

Substantiation is strict and unforgiving: a contemporaneous written acknowledgment under §170(f)(8) for gifts of $250 or more, Form 8283 for noncash gifts over $500, and a qualified appraisal above $5,000 (publicly traded securities exempted).
DAF grants may not satisfy enforceable pledges or return benefits — event tickets, priority seating, memberships carrying value — and §4967 imposes excise taxes when they do.

authority.note: The AGI percentage ceilings — a permanent 60 percent for cash to public charities, 30 percent for long-term capital-gain property.
The 0.5-percent-of-contribution-base floor on itemizers' charitable deductions for tax years beginning after 2025.
The five-year carryforward for contributions above the percentage ceilings.
The donor-advised-fund definition — donor advisory privileges over a fund owned by a sponsoring public charity.
The contemporaneous written acknowledgment requirement, strictly enforced with no substantial-compliance rescue.
Concededly genuine gifts denied because the acknowledgment letter omitted the required no-goods-or-services statement — the substantiation statute means what it says.
Excise taxes on more-than-incidental benefits that flow back from DAF grants.
Noncash reporting above $500 and the appraisal rules, with the publicly-traded-securities exception.

requirements: A genuine multi-year giving pattern — bunching rearranges gifts the client already intends; it does not manufacture generosity.
Cash flow or an appreciated-securities position deep enough to fund several years at once.
A DAF account at a sponsoring organization, opened ahead of the custodian's year-end transfer cutoffs.
The discipline to take the standard deduction in off years rather than leak additional itemized gifts.
risks: The leading challenge is substantiation, and it is purely mechanical: a missing or defective §170(f)(8) acknowledgment kills the deduction regardless of proof of payment — Durden v. Commissioner denied concededly real church gifts over the letter's wording.
DAF contributions are irrevocable — the funds are committed to charity for good even though grant timing stays advisory.
The 30 percent ceiling can push part of a large stock gift into carryforward years; model AGI headroom before funding, not after.
Stock held one year or less deducts at basis, not value — verify holding periods before placing the transfer order.
Grants that touch pledges, tickets, or member benefits invite §4967 excise exposure and damage the sponsor relationship.
stateNotes: Conformity: most states with itemized-deduction regimes conform to the federal charitable deduction, but several cap or disallow itemized deductions outright — the state-side value of bunching varies far more than the federal side.
PTET interaction: none — this is an individual itemized deduction, and no pass-through entity tax election touches it.

Missouri: itemizing on the Missouri return is available only when the taxpayer itemizes federally, and the Missouri standard deduction equals the federal amount (RSMo §143.131), so the bunch-year/off-year rhythm swings the Missouri return in step with the federal one.
reviewChecklist: Bunch size tested against the 60/30 percent ceilings and the 0.5 percent floor at projected AGI.
Holding period and basis verified for any securities slated for transfer; custodian cutoff dates calendared.
Acknowledgment-letter and Form 8283 obligations assigned and tracked through to receipt.
No outstanding enforceable pledges earmarked for satisfaction by DAF grants.
Off-year plan documented: standard deduction, no stray itemized gifts.

client.teaser: Same giving, bigger deduction — the only change is the calendar.
client.headline: Give the same amount to charity and deduct more of it
plainEnglish: Charitable gifts only help your taxes when all your deductions together beat the standard deduction. In 2026 that bar is $32,200 for a married couple. If you give $10,000 a year, much of it may be doing nothing for your tax bill.

The fix is timing. Put three years of gifts — say $30,000 — into a donor-advised fund in one year. That big number clears the bar and gets counted. In the off years, you take the standard deduction. Your charities notice nothing: the fund sends their usual gift each year, on your instructions.
There is a bonus move. Fund the account with stock that has grown, instead of cash. You deduct the full current value, and the tax on the growth never comes due — not for you, not for the charity.
One new wrinkle: starting in 2026, a small first slice of gifts does not count in each year you itemize. Bunching means you pay that toll once every few years instead of every year.
client.analogy: It is like a rewards card that only counts big visits. Three medium trips earn nothing. The same total spent in one visit earns the reward — so you shop once and stock the pantry.
benefits: More total deductions for exactly the same giving
Your charities still receive their gift every year
Donating winning stock skips the tax on its growth
One account holds all the receipts and paperwork
steps: WE size the bunch and pick the best year for it.
WE help open the fund account and plan any stock transfer ahead of the custodian's cutoff.
YOU fund it once — cash or the shares we select together.
YOU advise the fund's annual grants to your charities; WE track the receipts and file the forms.
clientCommitments: Fund the account before the year-end cutoff — stock transfers take time
Keep the fund's acknowledgment letters with your tax records
Hold off on extra itemized gifts in the off years

annualMaintenance: Confirm bunch-year vs. off-year status and reset withholding or estimates to match
Track acknowledgment letters and Form 8283 filings in bunch years
Re-run the AGI-ceiling and floor math whenever income changes
deliverables: Bunching schedule laying out the deduction across the full cycle
Funding memo (cash vs. appreciated securities) with custodian instructions
Substantiation checklist with retained acknowledgment letters
